content: The breast is composed of milk-producing glands, which are organized into units called lobules. These glands are connected by a network of ducts that converge to form a common drainage pathway, ultimately leading to the nipple. Surrounding the nipple is a pigmented area of tissue known as the areola. The structure of the breast is supported by fibro-elastic and fatty tissue, which also help maintain its distinctive shape. The breast itself lies atop the pectoral muscle, which rests on the thoracic cage. The boundaries of the breast are as follows: Superiorly: the clavicle Inferiorly: the inframammary crease (commonly referred to as the bra line) Medially: the sternum Laterally: the axilla Each breast contains a network of lymphatic tissue, with approximately 90% of lymphatic drainage directed to the lymph nodes in the ipsilateral axilla. The remaining 10% drains into the internal thoracic nodes located beneath the sternum, which are not accessible during a physical examination. These lymphatic pathways are clinically significant in the context of breast cancer, as they are often the first sites of metastatic spread. Breast examinations are typically performed on women, as breast diseases, particularly cancer, are far more common in women than in men. Malignancies usually originate in either the glandular tissues responsible for milk secretion or the ductal structures that transport milk to the nipple. Breast examinations can be conducted by a clinician (Clinical Breast Exam, or CBE) or by the patient themselves (Self Breast Exam, or SBE). For asymptomatic women, clinical breast exams are generally performed annually starting at age 40, coinciding with the increased risk of breast cancer development. Risk factors for breast cancer include early onset of menstruation, never having been pregnant, older age at first pregnancy, and older age at menopause. Self-breast exams are often recommended on a monthly or less frequent basis, as they may help detect cancer at an earlier stage, potentially reducing cancer-related morbidity and mortality. However, mammography, with or without a clinical breast exam, has stronger evidence supporting its routine use as a screening tool for early detection of malignancy. In symptomatic patients, the goal of the breast examination is to better characterize the abnormality, identify its underlying cause, and guide further evaluation and treatment. Symptoms related to the breast may include: Discrete masses detected by the patient, which are often concerning for malignancy. Pain, which may be associated with various conditions, including cyclic hormonal changes in menstruating women or, less commonly, malignancies. Unusual nipple discharge, such as: Bloody discharge, which raises concern for malignancy. Milk production in non-pregnant individuals, which may suggest inappropriate prolactin secretion from the pituitary gland or be induced by certain medications. Skin changes, such as: Redness, which may indicate infection or inflammation, such as mastitis in postpartum patients. Peau d'orange texture, resembling an orange peel, which is associated with an aggressive inflammatory malignancy. If a mass or abnormality is identified, its location can be described using one of four quadrants (upper outer, upper inner, lower outer, lower inner) or by imagining a clock face superimposed on the breast. It is important to note that breast symptoms may sometimes be caused by diseases in other parts of the body. For example, inappropriate milk production may result from a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor, and breast development in men may indicate underlying liver disease. Therefore, a thorough history and evaluation of other organ systems may be warranted. Breast examinations should be performed systematically to ensure all tissue is palpated. The patient should be lying flat, with one arm placed behind their head to allow easier access to the breast and axilla. Only the breast being examined should be uncovered. The examiner should observe for skin or nipple dimpling, retraction, discoloration, obvious masses, or asymmetry. Observing the breasts while the patient is sitting up may help detect asymmetry or surface abnormalities, particularly in individuals with larger breasts. Palpation of the breast and axilla should be conducted using the pads of the middle three fingers, applying steady pressure in a circular motion. The examiner should palpate to three levels of depth: superficial, medium, and deep (to the chest wall). The nipple and areolar regions should also be palpated. Normal breast tissue has a lumpy consistency due to the mix of lobular, ductal, and supporting tissues. The goal of the clinical breast exam is to identify masses that may be consistent with malignancy. Concerning masses often have the following characteristics: They feel different from the surrounding breast tissue (referred to as a dominant mass). They are firm, irregular, and have poorly defined borders. They may be fixed to adjacent tissue. They tend to increase in size over time. As breast density decreases with age (due to replacement of lobular tissue with fat), it becomes easier to identify masses in older patients. Three systematic methods for breast examination include: 1. Vertical Strips: The breast is divided into vertical strips, each palpated sequentially from the clavicle to below the breast, moving laterally to medially. 2. Pie or Radial Spoke Pattern: The breast is divided into pie-like slices, with the nipple at the center. Palpation starts at the nipple and moves outward toward the periphery of each slice. 3. Circular Pattern: Palpation begins at the nipple and proceeds in a spiral fashion toward the periphery. The axillary region should also be palpated, as axillary lymph nodes are often the first site of metastatic spread in breast cancer. The patient’s arm should be positioned to allow access to the axilla, and the examiner should palpate for abnormal nodules or lumps that could indicate axillary adenopathy. Most women will not have palpable axillary lymph nodes. If discrete masses are felt, their firmness, quantity, and mobility should be noted. Malignancy is often associated with firm, immobile, and adherent nodes. Additional aspects of the exam may include: Assessment of nipple discharge: Bloody discharge is particularly concerning for cancer, though most discharge is due to benign conditions. Evaluation of skin puckering or dimpling, which may suggest an underlying mass. Observation of nipple retraction, which may indicate a mass growing beneath the nipple. Assessment of redness or pain, which may suggest inflammation or infection. Examiners should be cautious when evaluating women with large breasts, as it can be technically challenging to ensure a thorough examination. Taking adequate time and systematically covering all areas of the breast is essential. Any discrete mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise, and further evaluation, including biopsy, is often required. Breast cancer can occur in men and in younger women, so concerning findings in these populations should also be appropriately evaluated. If there is any uncertainty regarding exam findings, input from an experienced clinician should be sought.
